title: only if
text: (This review was done pretty much immediately after release, so things may or may not have changed since.) I'm simply baffled by this game. I know this game is supposed to be surreal (think Stanley Parable or Kentucky Route Zero), but the game is extremely confusing and irritating to play. Walkthrough is pretty much needed, as the game doesn't give the player even an inkling of an idea when it comes to solving certain puzzles. So you begin the game by going to a party, but your vision fades to white at the door. You wake up in a strange bed with no recollection of past events, so you set to figure out what's happened. Except you're thrown into a weird dream like world that defies logic and natural laws. And you get shouted at by a voice in a radio doing a bad Al Pacino impression. The game looks decent enough. The game runs 60 FPS most of the time, but for some odd reason tanks to 30 and even below for no apparent reason. This kind of behavior happened in the second room of the game, but when later revisiting the room in another puzzle, the game ran at 60 FPS again. I have no idea as to why this happens, forced VSync, maybe? There seems to be only very primitive graphical controls with a handful of predetermined levels of graphical fidelity. There should be more detailed graphical options for tweaking things like texture quality, anti-aliasing, anisotropic filtering, VSync etc. The voice acting is susceptible to very annoying changes in audio level. The two types of voices you're going to hear are the main character and a mysterious voice on the radio. The main character seems to be clearly audible most of the time, but sometimes inaudibly mumbles something for no apparent reason. While this mumbling is annoying, the radio voice is even worse. Sometimes when the radio was far away, I couldn't make sense through the low audio level, distortion and unclear voice acting, whereas scenes where the radio was closer caused some clipping. In my case it got to the point of hurting my ears at certain points, especially when the radio voice was practically in my ear. The lack of captions didn't make understanding dialogue any easier. Controlling the character is easy enough in situations that don't require precise platforming. Unfortunately, there is some precise platforming involved in at least one section. The dimensions of how far or high the main character can jump are not really clear, and I fell to my death multiple times by either bumping my head on something or just falling short. The level layout is also very confusing, and many times I had to simply make a leap of faith to see if I could make a jump - and many times that failed. There seem to be also some invisible walls, which at least in one scenario made me think I hit a bug. The way the camera behaves can also be kind of dizzying and sickess inducing at times. Especially crouching while moving can cause some tilting (I guess roll is the correct term) that is exaggerated and very unnatural. The worst thing about Only If is the lack of direction. As of writing this review, I've been to seven or so sections. The game gives very little to no hints at all as to what you're supposed to do. Actually, I'd go even further and say that the game even misleads you. It's difficult in a review to point out these sorts of things without spoilers, and I'd like to keep this spoiler free. I'm only going to say that the game wants the player to name a thing at one point. The game primes you by displaying some scenery associated to one thing, but then expects a completely different answer. Also, there's a button mashing sequence that, as far as I can tell, leads only to the main characters death and a level restart. Creating an experience that is not frustratingly obscure to the player is something I expect from any game, surreal or not. The worst challenges in this game are not just stopping and thinking about all the mechanics of a puzzle, or trial and error, or even memorizing. The challenge at its worst is truly in the realm of "guess the developer logic" type of "puzzling". I simply cannot recommend this game in it's current form.

text: Played this game on console until the wheels fell off and being able to play it once in a while is the only real reason I keep my old 360. $2.49 is cheap, though, it looks so much better on PC and there's a few decent mods for it so I decided to buy it and maybe I'll sell my console that otherwise only collects dust and mounds of cat fur. It is a good game but the AI is kinda trash. Don't even think about letting it drive anything and don't think that enemy officer you can barely see with your scope can't hit you with the pea shooter pistol he's carrying. Cuz he can and will headshot you from 300 meters away, while you're laying down in the grass peeking around a boulder the size of a Volkswagen... AT NIGHT! The enemy AI is WAAAAAY overpowered in this game. Those ♥♥♥♥ers see you coming and can draw a bead on you before you've even left the enlistment office back in the states! Other than this, expect to see your AI squaddies getting hung up on rocks, taking cover beside objects instead of behind them, and everyone's (including your own) reloading and positioning animations happen with a speed and urgency you'd expect to see on a Sunday morning at the firing range. Seriously, I can load 5 rounds into a bolt action rifle one bullet at a time in the comfort and safety of my back yard faster than these "elite soldiers" can swap a mag in a firefight, and that's a fact. It's still a fun game, though. The missions are intense and brutal, and you will die a lot. Your squadmates, even more so, including the occasional and deliberate battlefield suicide if the pressure is too great. You're also going to run a lot so take care of your feet. And be warned: You will have to monkey around with the files to force it to run an earlier version if you're going to try to mod it. I would never pay the full $10 for this game, it's just too old, but for $2.49? Damn right! Red River, though? Not worth a nickel.

title: operation flashpoint: dragon rising
text: Much like the 2012 movie 'Dredd', this game didn’t get the acclaim it should have, for it was and still is (to some degree) brilliant. Operation Flashpoint: Dragon Rising is a detailed tactical shooter making efforts to model realistic soldiering on the battlefield. I've had a lot of fun playing this game with a friend, prior to its release through steam, where voice communication was essential to detail enemy positions (and more) while heading towards objectives, defending a location or were simply being chased as we searched for a landing zone extraction. The graphics are fantastic for a game of this age, and certainly stand up well in comparison to more modern games. However, there is no developer support for the game now, nor is it possible to play [large] player verses player game modes, but when it comes to playing the cooperative campaign it works well and for this reason alone the game is great. So is the game worth getting? Well, if you are looking for a tactical, realistic 2 player coop shooter and see this in the sale, then yes, it's worth getting.

title: operation flashpoint: red river
text: Despite there being many perfectly valid criticisms thrown its way, I have to say I still like it. For once - it doesn't have regenerating health - instead, you bleed until you patch yourself up (and then use the the infinite medkit you have, but I guess life isn't perfect). The main problem with it is that it took on the name of a franchise reknowned for its focus on vehicle use and squad (i.e. 8-10 people) tactics taking place in a large open environment. People unfamiliar with the Flashpoint name wouldn't care if Codemasters just called it "Red River" and those who are ended up brewing a turn storm around the game. Other flaws include glitchy grapchis and overall shoddy optimization, but not to the gamebreaking level. Character models look nice, with lots of detail on the marine characters, missions take place across large patches of terrain, and although you are confined to a certain area battlefield-style, it rarely becomes an issue. Missions also sport long rides in the back of a humvee, where the only thing you do is listen to the tutorial voice in the form of your platoon's staff sergeant. These rides are tedious, but wrighting is decent and the guy is genuinely hilarious  at times (provided you've ever been in the military or are a fan of Generation Kill), and he reminds me of a sergeant in my old unit. Speaking of Generation Kill - both this game and the previous one (Dragon Rising) rip entire dialogues straight out of the show - I guess they ran out of creativity half-way through writing the story. Most annoying of all - the AI. While friendlies can take a little getting used to, but once you get the hang of commanding them they can be made to function, the enemy AI all graduated from the Tajik special ed class and handed an AK - they either stand in the same spot doing nothing or run towards you. Taking cover is also an overly complicated concept for them. Not only that, but they take damage like a china teacup in a bull arena - you'll be lucky to kill one before he♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥himself on a thornbush and bleeds to death. All in all, the game feels very reminiscent of the Brothers in Arms games, except that actual terrain was used for the levels instead of them looking like a collection of conveniently placed chest-high walls. But I wish they ripped a few more elements off that franchise as well, like the gun accuracy and sway, and maybe the unlobotomized AI while they're at it.

title: orcs must die! 2
text: The first Orcs Must Die! was an amazing action/tower defense hybrid and the second adds to the awesomeness. Another playable character with different weapons and traps, more weapons and traps, more levels, endless mode, and coop make this an improvement on an already excellent game. The only real issue with this game is that some of the levels are obviously designed for coop play and can be frustrating to play solo. I generally prefer the levels from the original game because of this. They also removed the ballista from the game and nerfed the mace trap so it's much less useful (but still costs just as much). The dlc adds several nice items, traps and levels so I would recommend to just get the whole franchise pack and be done with it. As an aside, it looks like this is the end of Orcs Must Die! as we know it. The developer is working on a new Orcs Must Die!  game, but they're turning it into a free to play MOBA. I'm disappointed in their decision, but this game is still excellent and I recommend you get it if you're at all interested.

text: A brilliant follow up of the first title. It has what the first one was criticised for not having - Horde mode and Multiplayer, yet it retains a challenging gameplay on higher difficulty levels. Thumbs up, the devs have listened to the feedback provided by reviews and worked on it. The game performs really well even on my calculator. (I can barely run modern games, but with Orcs Must Die 2, the fps drop is noticeable only with many characters and spells rampaging during the end stages of the horde mode.) The game can be quite expensive with all the dlcs, but the sales are not unusual. Well done!

text: After being asked to give the game another shot by the devs, I decided to give the game another chance. Gone is the heavy pvp focus from my original time with the beta.  The game is classic OMD! and for the most part is a fairly authentic experience.  I have a few gripes, such as the convoluted leveling systems, and the lack of emphasis on careful trap planning.  There just isn't enough time to get a good feel of the level before the orcs start spawning. That said, OMDU retains some of the charm that made the first two games as fun as they were.  The orcs themselves aren't as well fleshed out, I hardly ever hear them question why they're being obliterated en masse, and that was part of the fun of killing the little guys.  However, the main characters are still spouting goofy one-liners.  Traps feel like they hit a lot harder than they did in the previous games, which is nice. Overall, I feel like the first two games were better, but OMDU may be worth your time if you're looking to try a unique game and you haven't played the first two.  It's definitely a better game than it was when I first reviewed it.
